title: Beyond awareness
statement: A thought can influence you before you know it is there.
explanation: Freud distinguished mental life from conscious awareness. In his theory, wishes, memories and conflicts can shape actions without entering the account a person gives of them.
nuance: Imagine sincerely believing a meeting is unimportant, then repeatedly forgetting it. Freud would ask whether another intention is competing with the stated one. That is a question about possible conflict, not proof that every lapse reveals a secret. His unconscious is a theoretical account of mental processes, not a second little person hidden inside the skull.
metaphor: A moving line beneath a floor nudges open a hatch while the visible surface seems still.

composition.description: A moving line beneath a floor nudges open a hatch while the visible surface seems still.

title: The closed door
statement: Keeping something out of awareness does not remove its pressure.
explanation: Freud called repression the exclusion of an unacceptable mental representative from consciousness. The excluded material remains active in his model, finding indirect expression through symptoms or dreams.
nuance: Repression differs from deciding to put a worry aside: deliberate suppression is conscious. In Freud's account, the person may not know what is being avoided or how. A symptom can be a costly detour around a conflict, rather than a message with one easy translation. Repressed material is not necessarily an accurate record of a forgotten event.
metaphor: A knot presses against a shut doorway; a line bends underneath and emerges on the other side.

composition.description: A knot presses against a shut doorway; a line bends underneath and emerges on the other side.

title: Two intentions
statement: Sometimes the sentence takes the turn you did not plan.
explanation: Freud treated certain slips of speech as collisions between intentions. A competing thought can distort the intended sentence rather than replacing it with a perfectly candid confession.
nuance: If a host accidentally says a gathering is closed while opening it, Freud asks whether reluctance has entered the greeting. Fatigue and ordinary language errors remain possible explanations. A slip is neither a lie detector nor a reliable window into someone's deepest desires. Its significance, in his method, depends on associations and the surrounding situation.
metaphor: A sentence approaches a barrier and branches into an unintended phrase below.

composition.description: A sentence approaches a barrier and branches into an unintended phrase below.

title: An uneasy agreement
statement: A symptom may serve both a wish and the force that opposes it.
explanation: For Freud, many neurotic symptoms were compromise formations. They allowed a disguised satisfaction while also meeting the demand that the underlying wish be restrained or punished.
nuance: A repeated ritual might reduce anxiety while keeping the unresolved fear central to the person's day. Freud interprets such patterns through competing forces, rather than simple willpower. This historical account does not explain every symptom, and recognizing a possible conflict does not establish its cause. A symptom can have several determinants at once.
metaphor: Two taut threads enter a knot; neither thread wins, and the knot keeps tightening.

composition.description: Two taut threads enter a knot; neither thread wins, and the knot keeps tightening.

title: What the dream shows
statement: The dream you remember is not the same as the thoughts used to interpret it.
explanation: Freud called the remembered dream its manifest content. The latent dream-thoughts are the associations and concerns reconstructed through interpretation, not a second dream waiting intact behind the first.
nuance: Dreaming of a locked station could lead one person to a missed journey and another to a family farewell. Freud's method begins with the dreamer's associations to particular details. The distinction between manifest and latent does not license an interpreter to invent any hidden story they like. It names a hypothesis about transformation that must be argued for.
metaphor: An image rests above a waterline; several branching associations become visible underneath.

composition.description: An image rests above a waterline; several branching associations become visible underneath.

title: Many into one
statement: A single dream image can carry several trains of thought.
explanation: In Freud's account, condensation lets different people, memories or concerns converge in one dream element. The strange composite is dense because more than one association contributes to it.
nuance: A dream figure might have a colleague's face, a parent's voice and a stranger's coat. Freud would investigate the associations to each feature rather than search for one person the figure really is. Condensation helps explain why a brief dream can generate a long analysis. It does not establish that every image has a concealed message.
metaphor: Three independently drawn streams converge in one irregular form, without losing their separate origins.

composition.description: Three independently drawn streams converge in one irregular form, without losing their separate origins.

title: The misplaced weight
statement: The smallest detail can carry the strongest feeling.
explanation: Freud proposed that dream-work shifts emotional emphasis from important thoughts to less threatening details. A dream's apparent center can therefore differ from what matters in the associated waking conflict.
nuance: A dream about a misplaced cup might carry the anger connected with an argument that barely appears in the dream. The cup itself need not be a universal symbol. Displacement is Freud's explanation of how emphasis changes during dream formation. It is a way to investigate disproportionate feeling, not a rule that a trivial object always hides something dramatic.
metaphor: A charge crosses from a large faint circle to a small ordinary one, making the small circle visibly heavier.

composition.description: A charge crosses from a large faint circle to a small ordinary one, making the small circle visibly heavier.

title: Thought becomes scene
statement: A dream must find pictures for thoughts that are not pictures.
explanation: Freud described dream-work as transforming thoughts into forms that can be represented, especially visual scenes. Abstract relations may become situations, spatial arrangements or actions.
nuance: A concern about exclusion might appear as being left outside a building. The picture is a possible rendering of a thought, not a fixed dictionary entry: a building has different associations for different dreamers. Freud emphasizes that interpretation works against this transformation, asking how a scene could be connected to thoughts rather than taking the image literally.
metaphor: An abstract written thought crosses an empty space and is redrawn as a small house with a closed door.

composition.description: An abstract written thought crosses an empty space and is redrawn as a small house with a closed door.

title: The story afterwards
statement: The mind can make a coherent account from material that arrived in fragments.
explanation: Freud called secondary revision the work that organizes dream material into something resembling a comprehensible story. The dream's smooth narrative can conceal discontinuities in its formation.
nuance: On waking, someone may connect two disjointed scenes with an explanation that was not clearly present during sleep. Freud also treated secondary revision as part of dream formation, not merely a reporting error after waking. A neat story is therefore something to examine, rather than proof that all its elements were generated in that order or for that purpose.
metaphor: Separate uneven panels drift together; seam lines appear later and make the fragments look like a sequence.

composition.description: Separate uneven panels drift together; seam lines appear later and make the fragments look like a sequence.

title: A wish in disguise
statement: Freud asked how a dream might stage the satisfaction of a wish.
explanation: Wish-fulfilment is central to Freud's dream theory. A child's dream of eating a forbidden treat is the simple case; adult dreams, he argued, often disguise wishes through conflict and distortion.
nuance: An unpleasant dream does not automatically refute Freud's theory on its own terms: he proposed that different parts of the mind can respond differently to the same wish. But this flexibility makes the claim difficult to test. He later confronted traumatic repetition more directly. The card describes his historical theory, not a settled explanation of every dream.
metaphor: A waking figure remains apart from an unattainable object; drawn paths form an imagined encounter overhead.

composition.description: A waking figure remains apart from an unattainable object; drawn paths form an imagined encounter overhead.

title: The pause has a history
statement: The difficulty of saying something may belong to the thing being approached.
explanation: Freud called the forces opposing analytic work resistance. Silence, forgetting or dismissing an association could matter because they occurred near material that was difficult to acknowledge.
nuance:
A person may remember many details yet find one topic abruptly uninteresting. Freud would explore that shift rather than insist that reluctance proves guilt. Resistance is an interpretation of a relation to painful material, not permission to disregard a person's boundaries. Fatigue, disagreement and mistrust also have ordinary explanations.

The useful question is what becomes difficult here, and why. Calling every objection resistance would make the theory impossible to challenge.
metaphor: An open gate swings partly shut as a thought approaches, showing interference rather than simple absence.

composition.description: An open gate swings partly shut as a thought approaches, showing interference rather than simple absence.

title: Both at once
statement: Love and hostility can concern the same person.
explanation: Freud used ambivalence to describe opposed emotional tendencies toward one object. Affection does not necessarily cancel anger, and anger does not prove that affection was false.
nuance:
Someone can miss a parent while also feeling relieved by their absence. The feelings concern different aspects of one relationship. Freud treated such conflict as important in symptoms and mourning; it is not a diagnosis in itself.

Ambivalence differs from indecision between two alternatives. The issue is that the same person is loved and resented, sometimes with one tendency kept out of awareness. A single emotional label may be less accurate than acknowledging the contradiction.
metaphor: A beam tilts between two suspended weights without dropping either side.

composition.description: A beam tilts between two suspended weights without dropping either side.

title: A divided intention
statement: An action can have more than one psychological purpose.
explanation: Freud sought conflicting motives behind behavior that appeared pointless or inconsistent. In his account, an act can express one intention while frustrating another, without either being fully conscious.
nuance:
A person who longs for closeness may repeatedly arrive late to the meeting that could provide it. Freud might investigate whether attachment also brings feared dependence. That hypothesis would require context, not just the lateness.

The point is not that people secretly want every bad outcome they encounter. Conflict can shape a response without explaining the external circumstances. Harm and misfortune should not be translated automatically into unconscious consent.
metaphor: A single route divides into two paths that pull in different directions.

composition.description: A single route divides into two paths that pull in different directions.

title: The apparently accidental
statement: Freud asked whether an ordinary mistake might be psychologically connected.
explanation: His study of everyday errors extends psychoanalytic inquiry beyond obvious illness. Forgetting a name, losing an object or misspeaking may, he argued, be related to other thoughts and intentions.
nuance:
An unwanted appointment might be forgotten while a pleasant one is remembered. Freud looks for a pattern and the person's associations; one isolated lapse proves little. Attention, language habits and chance remain relevant explanations.

Psychic determinism is stronger than the everyday observation that motives sometimes influence mistakes. It belongs to Freud's historical explanatory program. Reading significance into an event does not independently demonstrate the proposed cause.
metaphor: An apparently isolated dot becomes connected to a winding chain of remembered associations.

composition.description: An apparently isolated dot becomes connected to a winding chain of remembered associations.

title: More than one cause
statement: One symptom can gather several histories.
explanation: Freud described symptoms and dream elements as overdetermined: more than one chain of association contributes to them. Interpretation therefore need not end when the first plausible connection is found.
nuance:
A fear surrounding travel might be connected with separation, an earlier fright and a current conflict about leaving someone behind. These connections can coexist in Freud's account. They are not interchangeable with proof of medical causation.

Overdetermination also complicates the idea of a single hidden key. A compelling story can be incomplete. The same pattern may have different meanings in different lives, and an interpretation needs to remain open to revision.
metaphor: Several independently drawn paths meet in one knot, each retaining its own entry point.

composition.description: Several independently drawn paths meet in one knot, each retaining its own entry point.

title: A real effect, an imagined scene
statement: An imagined event can matter without having happened.
explanation: Freud distinguished psychical reality from material reality. Fantasies can organize desire, fear and guilt even when the events depicted are not historical occurrences.
nuance:
Someone can feel guilty about a hostile wish without having harmed the person involved. The feeling has psychological reality; it does not turn the imagined action into an actual event.

This distinction is essential when discussing memory and interpretation. An emotionally convincing account is not, by itself, evidence that a particular event occurred. Freud's changing views on fantasy and trauma are part of the history of psychoanalysis, rather than a reason to dismiss real experiences of abuse.
metaphor: A faint imagined figure leaves a visible mark inside a present figure while the two remain spatially separate.

scene.caption: a real effect, an imagined scene

composition.description: A faint imagined figure leaves a visible mark inside a present figure while the two remain spatially separate.

title: Yesterday remains
statement: Recent impressions give a dream material to work with.
explanation: Freud noticed that dreams often incorporate details from the preceding day. He called these day-residues: recent thoughts or impressions that connect with other concerns during dream formation.
nuance:
A passing advertisement can furnish a dream's setting while an older worry supplies its emotional force. In Freud's account, recent material and earlier wishes become linked; the visible reference to yesterday need not explain everything.

This is different from claiming that each dream is a coded prediction. The detail belongs to remembered experience. Freud's theory concerns how memories are selected and transformed, not supernatural information received during sleep.
metaphor: A recent small detail passes through a gate and connects with branching older associations.

composition.description: A recent small detail passes through a gate and connects with branching older associations.

title: Start with the detail
statement: A dream image means more when the dreamer speaks around it.
explanation: Freud asked people to report associations to separate dream elements. His method differs from assigning each image one universal meaning before hearing about the person's life.
nuance:
A bridge might lead to a childhood walk, an argument or a phrase heard yesterday. These associations matter because they connect this image to this dreamer's concerns. An interpreter should not simply announce what bridges mean.

Freud also proposed recurring symbols, so his practice was not purely individual association. The tension between those approaches remains worth noticing. A plausible interpretation should explain its route through the material rather than rely on the interpreter's authority.
metaphor: A small dream detail begins a winding thread on which memories appear in sequence.

composition.description: A small dream detail begins a winding thread on which memories appear in sequence.

title: Why the disguise?
statement: Freud treated distortion as the trace of a conflict.
explanation: Dream-censorship is Freud's name for forces that prevent certain wishes from appearing plainly. His theory explains an obscure dream as a transformed compromise, rather than a wish stated directly.
nuance:
A hostile feeling toward someone valued might appear through an unrelated character or an altered situation. Freud would connect the disguise with conflict, using the dreamer's associations.

Censorship is a metaphor for mental processes, not an actual guard inspecting thoughts. It is also a contested explanation, especially when any counterexample can be redescribed as further disguise. The useful distinction is between what appears in the dream and the argument offered for why it appears that way.
metaphor: A direct line meets a narrow doorway and finds a curved route beneath it.

composition.description: A direct line meets a narrow doorway and finds a curved route beneath it.

title: The unfinished interpretation
statement: A dream need not become completely transparent.
explanation: Freud acknowledged a point in dreams where associations become tangled and interpretation reaches a limit. A network of thoughts can extend beyond anything a single account fully reconstructs.
nuance:
The last unresolved detail is not necessarily a failure of effort. Freud described a dream's connections as branching into the larger life of thought. Interpretation can illuminate some relations without producing a final translation.

This restraint matters because a confident explanation can be mistaken for exhaustive knowledge. The dreamer may find a connection useful while still questioning the theory used to explain it. Understanding is partial, and unresolved material need not be forced into a neat ending.
metaphor: Several roots disappear beyond the lower edge beneath one remembered dream image.

composition.description: Several roots disappear beyond the lower edge beneath one remembered dream image.
